tagline: Shortgrass, two buttes, and towns at the end of everything.
intro: Out of Ault the byway runs east on Highway 14 to Briggsdale, then goes by highway and dusty county road across the Pawnee National Grassland by way of Grover, out to Raymer and on toward Sterling and Fort Morgan, 128 miles in all. This is shortgrass prairie, home to coyotes, prairie dogs, rattlesnakes and pronghorn.

The land saw a little farming early in the 20th century and was taken out of it after the Dust Bowl. Railroad towns sprang up, flourished and declined. Keota, on the old Prairie Dog Express, once had its water brought in by rail car.

moments.title: Grover
moments.text: Willa Cather put it at the end of everything in a story of 1900, and by 2020 it had grown almost 15 percent, to 157 people.

moments.title: Pawnee Buttes
moments.text: Two buttes stand about 300 feet above the plains, remnants of an old High Plains surface, soft clay under a sandstone cap, reached by a foot trail.

moments.title: Raymer
moments.text: Colorado calls it Raymer, but the Postal Service calls it New Raymer, as it has since the town's second start in 1909, and refuses to deliver to the other name.

practical: The unpaved county roads carry heavy truck traffic. Watch for flying dirt and rocks.

sources.label: Colorado Department of Transportation, Pawnee Pioneer Trails
